assertion: Since 2025, at least four states, including Oklahoma, have enacted restrictions on medical malpractice suits.
reason: Four states verified: Arkansas Act 124 (Feb 2025), Utah HB 503 (2025), New Mexico HB 99, Oklahoma SB 453 (effective Sept 1, 2025, general noneconomic cap).
searched: Oklahoma 2025 medical malpractice law enacted noneconomic damages cap restrictions

assertion: In 2025, Arkansas limited malpractice claims stemming from childbirth to five years; other claims involving children can still be filed until a minor's 11th birthday or two years post-injury, whichever is later.
reason: Act 124 section 4: childbirth injuries by the minor's fifth birthday; others the later of 11th birthday or two years.

assertion: New Mexico capped punitive damages ... and raised the standard of proof, requiring "clear and convincing" evidence for punitive damages.
reason: HB 99 section 41-5-7.1: clear and convincing evidence; punitive awards capped by reference to the compensatory limit.

assertion: Utah added protections shielding physicians' personal assets.
reason: Utah HB 503 (2025) bars collecting malpractice judgments from an individual provider's personal assets, with exceptions.
searched: Utah 2025 2026 law medical malpractice personal assets physicians judgment protect legislature

assertion: The state has capped noneconomic damages in malpractice cases at $450,000 since 2010, but it does not cap punitive damages.
reason: Utah Code 78B-3-410: $450,000 for causes of action arising on or after May 15, 2010. A search of the punitive-damages chapter found no cap; a 2026 bill (SB 227) proposes one, status unconfirmed.

assertion: Medicaid covered roughly 40% of births in 2024.
reason: CDC final 2024 data: Medicaid paid for 40.2% of deliveries.

assertion: The group has counted at least 146 hospitals that have stopped delivering babies or plan to stop from the end of 2020 through this year.
inaccuracy: The article says 146; CHQPR's report says 144 have stopped and 4 more announced stops by early 2027 (148). 'At least 146' is consistent but the report's own figure differs.
reason: Read the CHQPR PDF and site directly.

assertion: Fewer than a third of the state's counties had a birthing hospital as of July, according to the policy nonprofit Arkansas Center for Health Improvement.
reason: Search results report 22 of Arkansas's 75 counties with a birthing hospital (29%); the ACHI page itself did not expose the figure.
searched: Arkansas Center for Health Improvement birthing hospitals counties July 2026 fewer than a third

assertion: Idaho, which had lost more than a third of its OB-GYNs two years after its near-total abortion ban took effect in 2022, ...
reason: JAMA Netw Open study (PMC copy): Idaho lost 94 of 268 OB-GYNs practicing obstetrics (35%), net, Aug 2022 to Dec 2024. The study also cites recruiting difficulty, consolidation and no in-state residency.

sources.title: PMC copy of the JAMA Network Open study

assertion: In Virginia, voters approved a constitutional amendment that protects abortion rights and bars the state from prosecuting physicians who perform the procedure. Missouri voters upheld abortion rights, and Nevada voters added them; Idaho voters rejected a proposal to restore access.
reason: Virginia's text bars penalizing or prosecuting individuals for aiding or assisting abortion; U.S. News tally: Idaho rejected 56-44, Nevada 64-36 and Virginia 62-38 approved, Missouri rejected the repeal measure.

assertion: That left in place a law putting doctors at risk of prison time for providing a pregnant patient with lifesaving care.
inaccuracy: The claim says the law endangers doctors for lifesaving care; the evidence shows Idaho's ban has an exception for preventing the patient's death and a 2025 state ruling and federal order broadened protection. Prison risk (2-5 years) applies to care outside that exception.

sources.title: Idaho Capital Sun on the 2025 legislative session

searched: Idaho abortion ban exception life of mother doctors prison

assertion: Monticello, as a federally qualified health center, is protected by the Federal Tort Claims Act from many medical malpractice claims.
reason: HRSA-deemed health centers get FTCA malpractice protection and patients must sue the United States. The article's linked house.gov page concerns FTCA protection for House members and staff, not health centers, so the citation does not support the sentence.

assertion: Steward Health Care sold the hospital to CommonSpirit Health in May 2023, along with four other Utah hospitals.
reason: Steward and CommonSpirit announced completion of the five-hospital sale May 1, 2023.

assertion: Last year, a judge found Steward Health Care liable for gross medical negligence and awarded the family $951 million; the judgment was entered by default after Steward withdrew from the case, and Steward filed for bankruptcy in 2024.
reason: Salt Lake Tribune: Judge Corum found Steward liable Aug 3, 2025, awarded $951 million, approved counsel's withdrawal in May 2025, and entered judgment by default; Steward filed Chapter 11 in May 2024. Collectibility is in question and about half the award is punitive.

sources.title: Becker's: Steward ordered to pay nearly $1B

assertion: It took nearly 12 hours for the then-19-year-old to get an emergency cesarean section after the monitor showed signs of fetal distress, according to court records.
reason: Court records not obtained. The Tribune reports admission about 10:30 p.m. Oct 12, Pitocin begun about five hours later, distress 'for hours', and a C-section just before 6 a.m. Oct 14, over a day after admission. That is consistent with, but does not state, a 12-hour distress-to-surgery interval.

why_no_page: No page states the 12-hour interval; the court docket was not reachable.

assertion: In the first five years of Azaylee's life, Zancanella said, her medical bills exceeded $1 million.
speaker: Anyssa Zancanella
reason: The Tribune copy describes ongoing care costs but no bill total; this is the mother's own statement.
searched: Zancanella Azaylee medical bills first five years
why_no_page: No page states a bill total.
why_not: The $1,000,000 and $1,500,000 passages in the Utah and New Mexico statutes concern insurance and deposit requirements, not Azaylee's medical bills, so they do not bear on this claim.

assertion: Arkansas has had only one birth injury lawsuit in the past 10 years.
speaker: Aaron Pilkington
reason: No docket count or independent source found; a sponsor's assertion offered to justify the bill, not flagged as unverified in the article. A Future Caucus analysis of the bill discusses the limitations change but gives no lawsuit count.

assertion: Such verdicts are "rarely, if ever, being paid fully."
speaker: Joanne Doroshow
reason: General empirical claim from an advocate; no dataset found. The Steward case is consistent with it but one case does not establish a rule.

why_no_page: No study located stating the share of verdicts paid in full.
